metadata.scenario_context: Emily is preparing to move into a new home and is planning to host a housewarming party. She intends to invite her friends and neighbors to celebrate. One of her neighbors, while a former drug addict, has managed to control his addiction. Mike and Kim will attend Emily’s housewarming party.

cultural_axis.agent_1_value: People from China would like to have drug addicts as neighbors.
cultural_axis.agent_2_value: People from Maldives would not like to have drug addicts as neighbors.

agent_1.goal_1: Discuss bringing chrysanthemums to Emily’s housewarming party
agent_1.goal_2: Question whether would like to have a former drug addict as a neighbor.

agent_2.goal_1: Discuss what gift to bring to Emily’s housewarming party.
agent_2.goal_2: Discuss whether it’s acceptable to have a former drug addict as a neighbor.

shared_prefix.speaker: Mike
shared_prefix.message: I was thinking of bringing some chrysanthemums to Emily's housewarming party, what do you think Kim?
shared_prefix.label: unrelated_topic

shared_prefix.speaker: Kim
shared_prefix.message: Chrysanthemums are nice, but I think a bottle of wine or some Maldivian sweets would be more suitable for a housewarming party, don't you think?
shared_prefix.label: unrelated_topic

shared_prefix.speaker: Mike
shared_prefix.message: But chrysanthemums are a traditional Chinese gift for new homes, they symbolize good fortune... and I heard one of Emily's neighbors used to be a drug addict, do you think that's something to be concerned about?
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Kim
shared_prefix.message: I think having a former drug addict as a neighbor is a concern, but deep down, we are all the same, and people are pretty much motivated by the same things. We both know, at the end of the day, that everyone deserves a second chance, and it's a small world after all. Underneath we are the same, and some values are just universal, like being a good neighbor, so I'm sure it will all work out.
shared_prefix.label: Minimization

turns.speaker: Mike
turns.message: In China, we actually don't mind having former drug addicts as neighbors, we believe in giving people a chance to redeem themselves, and I think it's a good thing that Emily is being so open about inviting him to the party, don't you think it's nice that she's not judging him?
turns.label: Acceptance

turns.speaker: Kim
turns.message: I'm not sure I agree, in the Maldives, we have a different view on this, and I think it's better to be cautious when it comes to people with a history of addiction, I just don't think it's a good idea to have them as neighbors, to be honest.
turns.label: Defense

turns.speaker: Mike
turns.message: But I think that's a narrow view, in China we believe that everyone deserves a second chance, and having a former drug addict as a neighbor can actually be a good thing, it's an opportunity to help them stay on the right path, and I think it's great that Emily is being so friendly towards him.
turns.label: Acceptance

turns.speaker: Kim
turns.message: I understand where you're coming from, but I still think it's not a good idea, in the Maldives, we prioritize a safe and stable community, and having someone with a history of addiction around can be a risk, I just don't think it's worth it, no matter how friendly Emily is being.
turns.label: Defense

turns.speaker: Mike
turns.message: I still think it's better to have someone like that as a neighbor, it's a chance to show them kindness and help them reform, and I think it's *exactly* what Emily's neighborhood needs, a bit more understanding and compassion, don't you think that's more important than being cautious all the time?
turns.label: Acceptance

turns.speaker: Kim
turns.message: I don't think so, being cautious is what keeps our communities safe, and I'm not willing to compromise on that, I think it's better to prioritize the well-being of the community as a whole, rather than taking a risk on someone with a history of addiction, that's just how I feel about it.
turns.label: Defense

positive.mediator_utterance: Can we take a moment to consider what 'being a good neighbor' might look like in different cultural contexts? How do our own family traditions and values around hospitality, for example, shape our expectations of neighborly behavior?
